title: The last range
hookLine: four years of learning; now the sources themselves, and a life that carries them
tomorrow: one scholar picked a short list for the whole faith. why those?

cards: A recipe video can show you every step of a dish in under a minute, and you still haven't tasted it. A lot of faith reaches people that way now: a clip about a verse, a quote card, a thread explaining what a hadith means.

Useful, the way a trail map is useful. For four years, this path has been a map like that: the pillars, the schools, the heart, the reports and their chains. This is the last range, and the question at its foot is simple.
Why open the source yourself, when someone has already summed it up?

teach.b: The Qur'an's own answer starts with its first command to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In Pickthall's translation: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth." Not listen to a summary.
Read. And the book keeps asking people to come close to its words.

In one surah: "Will they then not meditate on the Qur'an, or are there locks on the hearts?" Another says, in paraphrase, that it was sent down full of blessing so that people would ponder its verses.
Pondering is something nobody can do for you. So this year goes to the sources themselves: the forty hadith one scholar gathered, the Qur'an read closely, and then a life that carries what it says.
Here's ground Muslims share with a neighbor.
The first psalm, in the Hebrew Bible, praises the one whose delight is in God's teaching. In the JPS 1917 translation: "in His law doth he meditate day and night."

teach.h: ONE BOOK RECITED, ONE BOOK ARGUED.
teach.b: A Jewish reader and a Muslim reader are both told the same thing: don't just own the book, sit with it, again and again. And one honest difference.
Muslims hold the Qur'an to be Allah's own speech, recited in Arabic in every prayer, and a translation is understood as an explanation of its meanings, not the Qur'an itself.
Jewish study reads the written Torah beside the oral Torah, the sages' long conversation, argued in pairs. Both turn back to the text. They sit at different tables when they do.

how: Many Muslims read a portion of the Qur'an daily, in Arabic, in a translation of its meanings, or both; some keep a set time after the dawn prayer, and study circles read a passage together and talk it through.

games.q: a friend sends you a quote card: a line said to be from the Qur'an, with a big claim about it in the caption. you've got two minutes. what do you do first?
o: look up the verse itself and read the lines around it.
repost it; the caption sounds like it knows the verse.
find a longer video that explains the caption's claim.
games.why: the Qur'an's first command is read, and it asks people to ponder its verses. the source comes before anyone's caption about it.

practice: Open a Qur'an, a translation or an app anywhere at all, and read one verse slowly, out loud if you can. It isn't a sign or a message picked for you; it's just the first verse of a year spent with the source.
Stay with that one verse for the sit, and let one word in it stand out.

wordCard.voice: The last range: year five, the summit climb. Fewer summaries, more source, and a life that carries it.
